title: Distributed Key-Value Store (Dynamo-style)
problem: Design an always-writable, horizontally scaled key-value store with tunable consistency: N replicas, configurable W/R quorums, vector-clock conflict resolution, gossip membership, and anti-entropy repair.
summary: A peer-to-peer KV cluster in the Dynamo lineage and the book's recommended AP design. Keys are routed via a consistent-hash ring to N replicas. Writes succeed once W replicas ack, and reads wait for R; W+R>N guarantees strong consistency per the book. Concurrent writes are detected via vector clocks and the store returns siblings for client-side resolution. Gossip handles decentralized failure detection; sloppy quorum + hinted handoff keep writes available during temporary failures; Merkle-tree anti-entropy repairs permanent divergence. Per-replica storage uses the Cassandra write/read path from the book: commit log → memtable → SSTable on disk, with a Bloom filter to skip SSTables on reads. The dominant stance is AP: availability during partitions is non-negotiable, as opposed to a CP store (e.g. a bank).

functional: PUT(key, value, context) writes a value; context carries the vector clock observed on the last GET
GET(key) returns one value, or multiple sibling values when concurrent writes happened
DELETE(key) emits a tombstone that is GC'd after gc_grace_seconds
Tunable consistency per operation: caller picks W (write quorum) and R (read quorum) against replication factor N
Replication factor N, with keys placed on N consecutive nodes walking clockwise on a consistent-hash ring
Automatic sibling resolution via a user-supplied merge function (OR-Set for carts, G-Counter for counters, LWW fallback)
nonFunctional: Peak 30K ops/sec with 80/20 read/write mix and p99 under 10ms at W=2/R=2
99.99% availability — writes must succeed during single-AZ failure via sloppy quorum + hinted handoff
Durable: an ack'd write survives f concurrent node crashes where f < N - W + 1
Horizontally scalable to petabytes by adding nodes to the ring without downtime
Eventual convergence within seconds of a partition healing via read-repair + anti-entropy
Storage amplification under 2x with leveled compaction; bloom filters keep read amplification under 1.5 SSTables/read

assumptions: Replication factor N=3, tunable W+R (default W=2, R=2 → strong; W=1, R=1 → AP-maximal)
Coordinator fan-out per op: 3 RPCs (writes) or up to 3 (reads)
Dataset ~500M keys at ~1 KB each (~500 GB logical, ~1.5 TB with RF=3) across 6 replicas
Vector clocks: ~30 bytes overhead per key at steady state (3-replica cluster), up to 200B during churn
estimates: Per-coordinator CPU: 3 RPCs × 30K ops/sec / 10 coordinators ≈ 9K outbound RPCs/sec/coord — well within a single box.

Anti-entropy scan: Merkle tree with 2^15 leaves per replica → compare 32K hashes/pair → ~1 MB of Merkle data per pair, seconds to compare; full repair of divergent leaves bounded by disk throughput (~100 MB/s).
Gossip: O(log N) rounds to propagate a membership change; with 1s rounds and 6 nodes, convergence in ~3s.
Quorum failure probability at W=2/R=2 with 99.9% per-replica availability: (1 - 0.999)^2 ≈ 10^-6 — effectively negligible under independent failures.
Storage per replica: 500 GB data + 2 GB Bloom filters + ~500 MB of vector-clock metadata.

client.name: Client SDK
client.summary: Thin library that issues PUT/GET with a vector-clock context and handles sibling values on read.

sections.heading: Responsibilities
sections.body:
- Send `PUT key value context=<vclock>` and `GET key` to any coordinator
- Receive sibling values on reads when concurrent writes happened
- Resolve siblings via a user-supplied merge function (shopping cart: union carts; counter: max; generic: last-write-wins by timestamp as a fallback)

sections.heading: Why the client sees siblings
sections.body: The store refuses to silently pick a winner on concurrent writes — only the application knows the right merge semantics (e.g. shopping-cart *union* vs counter *max*). Siblings surface the conflict instead of hiding it.

sections.heading: Why this matters for beginners
sections.body: Strong consistency is not a knob you flip on a distributed KV — it's a quorum math choice. Understanding W + R > N is the single most important Dynamo insight.

bottlenecks.title: Sibling explosion under concurrent writers
bottlenecks.trigger: Hot keys (e.g. a shared shopping cart edited from multiple devices, or a fan-in counter) receive concurrent writes faster than clients can read-merge-write. With W=1/R=1 AP-maximal config and vclock overhead growing from ~30B to 200B during churn, sibling sets can balloon past dozens of versions per key.
bottlenecks.symptom: GET returns ever-larger sibling arrays; client CPU spent merging grows unbounded; PUT payloads inflate as vclock context accumulates entries per replica; in extreme cases the client's merge function OOMs or returns nonsensical unions.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Cap sibling count client-side (e.g. 10) and fall back to LWW by wall-clock timestamp beyond that; use CRDT-shaped values (OR-Set for carts, G-Counter for counters) so merge is associative and idempotent; coalesce rapid writes from the same client into a single PUT with debouncing (~100ms).
bottlenecks.detection: Emit a client metric `kv.get.sibling_count` histogram; alert when p99 > 5 or any key exceeds 20. Also track `kv.put.context_vclock_entries` — alert when it exceeds the book's recommended threshold (~10 entries).

bottlenecks.title: Stale context causing write amplification via forced siblings
bottlenecks.trigger: Client caches a vclock context and writes with it after a long gap (e.g. mobile client offline for minutes while other clients advanced the key). Every such PUT is concurrent with recent writes and manufactures a new sibling, even when the user intent is last-write-wins.
bottlenecks.symptom: Steady growth in sibling counts even with a single active user; increased read latency as coordinator must reconcile more versions; PUT→GET→PUT loops on every write to drain siblings.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Do a read-before-write for stale contexts (context age > 30s); attach a monotonic client-session ID to disambiguate same-user writes; expire cached contexts aggressively (TTL 10s) and force a fresh GET on expiry.
bottlenecks.detection: Client-side metric `kv.put.context_age_ms` histogram; alert when p50 > 5s. Correlate with `kv.get.sibling_count` — a rising ratio of siblings-per-unique-writer indicates stale-context churn.

bottlenecks.title: Coordinator affinity / no client-side retry hedging
bottlenecks.trigger: SDK pins to a single coordinator per connection. With coordinator failureRate 0.0005 and serviceTimeMs up to 6ms, at 30K ops/sec a single slow/failing coordinator causes ~15 ops/sec to hit p99 tail (>200ms coord timeout window during replica fan-out).
bottlenecks.symptom: Sporadic user-visible latency spikes to hundreds of ms or occasional timeouts when a coordinator degrades, even though the cluster as a whole is healthy; on-call sees client error budget burn without a corresponding server-side incident.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Maintain a pool of connections across ≥3 coordinators; implement request hedging — fire a second request to another coordinator at p95 latency (~20ms) and take the first response; exponential-backoff retry on NetworkError with jitter; health-check coordinators via periodic no-op GET.
bottlenecks.detection: Client metric `kv.op.latency_ms{coordinator=...}` per-coordinator p99; alert when any single coordinator's p99 exceeds cluster median × 3. Track `kv.op.hedge_win_rate` — a sudden rise signals a degraded coordinator.

prebuild.explanation: ## Why the Client SDK is here for *this* problem This KV store is explicitly **AP** (always-writable), which means when two users edit the same key at the same time, the store refuses to pick a winner — it keeps both versions as "siblings" and hands them back on the next read. Someone has to actually merge those siblings, and that someone can't be the server: only the application knows whether `cart:user42` should be a *union* of shopping carts, a *max* of counter values, or a last-write-wins fallback. The SDK is where that merge logic lives, along with the vector-clock bookkeeping (tracking `{replica1: 4, replica2: 2}` as opaque context the caller must echo back on the next PUT). Without the SDK, every application team would reinvent this, badly. ## What happens without it A naive client that just calls `PUT` and `GET` over HTTP will eventually read back an array of two values instead of one and crash, or worse, silently keep the first one and lose the user's cart addition. The operator sees no server-side error — the cluster is behaving correctly — but support tickets roll in about "items disappearing from my cart." The bad write then poisons replica state, and the anti-entropy worker dutifully propagates the wrong value to the other replicas. ## The numbers At 30K ops/sec with 80/20 read/write, that's ~6K writes/sec. Vector-clock context is ~30 bytes steady-state but up to 200B during churn. If the SDK didn't cache and echo context correctly, *every* write would look concurrent to the store, manufacturing siblings on 6,000 writes/sec — sibling sets would explode within minutes on any hot key. ## Trade-off Pushing conflict resolution to the client keeps the server simple and always-writable, but it makes the SDK non-trivial and forces application developers to think about merge semantics they'd rather ignore.

coord.name: Coordinator
coord.summary: Stateless router: hashes the key, looks up the preference list on the ring, fans out to replicas, collects quorums, returns to the client.

sections.heading: Responsibilities
sections.body:
1. Hash key to ring token (MurmurHash3 32-bit)
2. Ring.preference_list(token, N) → [r1, r2, r3]
3. Fan out PUT/GET to all N replicas in parallel
4. Wait for W acks (PUT) or R responses (GET)
5. On read, compare vector clocks → return value OR siblings

sections.heading: Sloppy quorum + hinted handoff
sections.body: Strict quorum blocks writes when a replica is down. Book recommends **sloppy quorum**: 'the system chooses the first W healthy servers for writes and first R healthy servers for reads on the hash ring. Offline servers are ignored.' Writes for a down replica are taken by a healthy neighbour and tagged with a hint (`for=replica2`) — this is **hinted handoff**. When the target recovers, the hint is forwarded and cleaned up. Keeps writes available under short-term failures.

sections.heading: CAP stance
sections.body: We are an **AP system**: under a network partition, we keep accepting reads and writes on the reachable side and reconcile later. Book contrasts this with a CP system (e.g. a bank): a CP store would block writes on n1/n2 when n3 is partitioned to keep data consistent. The 'CA' corner of CAP cannot exist in a real distributed system because partitions are unavoidable.

sections.heading: Stateless + replaceable
sections.body: Coordinators hold no durable state. Any-node coordinator (Cassandra) or dedicated tier (Dynamo). Here we model a dedicated tier.

gained: No dedicated coordinator tier to operate
Client can pick a closer coordinator for lower latency
lost: Storage replicas also do coordination CPU — noisy neighbour risk
Cross-DC coordination is harder to reason about

bottlenecks.title: Head-of-line blocking from slow replicas exhausting coordinator fan-out concurrency
bottlenecks.trigger: At 30K ops/sec across ~10 coordinators (~3K ops/sec each) with N=3 fan-out = 9K in-flight RPCs per coord. If one replica's p99 spikes from 10ms to 200ms (GC pause, compaction stall, disk saturation), in-flight requests pile up: 3K ops/sec × 0.2s = 600 stuck requests per coord waiting on the laggard, approaching the configured concurrency=5000 ceiling.
bottlenecks.symptom: Coordinator rejects or queues new client ops with 503/timeout even though 2 of 3 replicas are healthy and W=2/R=2 quorums should still be reachable; p99 client latency jumps cluster-wide when only a single replica is degraded.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Return to client as soon as W (or R) acks arrive and cancel/abandon the straggler RPC instead of holding its slot; add a per-replica circuit breaker that short-circuits to the next preference-list entry (sloppy quorum) when a replica's p99 exceeds 3× median; use bounded per-replica outbound queues (e.g. 500 in-flight per replica per coord) so one slow replica cannot consume the global 5000 concurrency budget.
bottlenecks.detection: Track `coord.inflight_rpcs{replica=...}` gauge and `coord.rpc_latency_ms{replica=...}` p99 per replica; alert when any single replica accounts for >40% of inflight RPCs or its p99 exceeds 50ms. Also alert on `coord.concurrency_utilization` > 70%.

bottlenecks.title: Hinted-handoff buffer accumulation during prolonged replica outage
bottlenecks.trigger: Under sloppy quorum, a coordinator diverts writes for a DEAD replica to a healthy neighbour tagged with hints. At 6K writes/sec cluster-wide × (1/3 of keys owned by the down replica) = 2K hinted writes/sec. A 1-hour outage produces ~7.2M hints × ~1KB ≈ 7.2GB of hint buffer; a multi-hour outage can exhaust hint-holder disk or cause replay storms on recovery.
bottlenecks.symptom: Healthy neighbours' disk usage climbs steadily during the outage; on recovery, the returning replica is flooded with hint replay traffic that competes with live writes, causing elevated write latency for 10+ minutes and possibly triggering a second cascading failure.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Cap per-coordinator hint buffer size (e.g. 5GB) and TTL (e.g. 3h) — beyond that, disable hinted handoff for that target and rely on anti-entropy/Merkle repair on recovery; throttle hint replay on recovery to ~10MB/s per sender; spread hint holders across multiple neighbours instead of single next-in-ring node.
bottlenecks.detection: Metric `coord.hints.pending_bytes{target=...}` and `coord.hints.pending_count{target=...}`; alert when any target's pending hints exceed 1GB or 1M entries, or when hint-buffer age p99 > 30 min.

bottlenecks.title: Stale ring version causing request storms during rebalance
bottlenecks.trigger: Gossip converges in ~3s for 6 nodes but coordinators fetch the authoritative ring lazily on version bump. During a rebalance (node join/leave), coordinators using ring_version=N send ops to replicas that have moved to version N+1; replicas reject with STALE_RING, coordinator re-fetches and retries. At 3K ops/sec per coord, even a 2s stale window produces ~6K rejected+retried ops per coord = instantaneous 2× amplification on an already-stressed cluster.
bottlenecks.symptom: Brief but sharp client latency spike (100–500ms) and elevated error rate every time a node joins/leaves or vnodes are rebalanced; on-call sees `STALE_RING` errors in logs correlated with membership churn.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Push ring updates proactively via gossip piggyback instead of lazy pull — coordinators subscribe to ring-version change events and pre-fetch before any op uses the new version; during rebalance, replicas serve ops under BOTH old and new ring for a grace window (e.g. 30s) rather than hard-rejecting; throttle rebalance vnode moves to bound blast radius.
bottlenecks.detection: Metric `coord.rpc.stale_ring_errors_total` rate and `coord.ring.version_lag_seconds` (time between gossip-announced version and coord-adopted version); alert when stale-ring error rate exceeds 1% of ops or version lag p99 > 5s.

prebuild.explanation: ## Why the Coordinator is here for *this* problem This is an AP key-value store with tunable W/R quorums — which means every single PUT and GET has to talk to multiple replicas (N=3), wait for enough of them to respond (W=2 or R=2), and then decide what to tell the client. *Someone* has to hash the key, look up which 3 replicas own it on the ring, fan out the RPCs in parallel, collect the quorum, and — on reads — compare vector clocks to detect siblings. That "someone" is the coordinator. It exists because the client shouldn't need to know the ring topology, track gossip membership, or implement quorum math, and the replicas shouldn't each have to reimplement fan-out logic. ## What happens without it If clients talked to replicas directly, every client SDK would need to embed a live copy of the ring, subscribe to gossip, handle ring-version mismatches during rebalances, and implement quorum collection. A single buggy client could hammer the wrong replica, miss a rebalance, or declare false failures. The user sees phantom unavailability; the operator sees a cluster that looks healthy but has clients mysteriously timing out; the replicas take the hit from misrouted traffic. ## The numbers At 30K ops/sec with N=3 fan-out, that's 90K RPCs/sec across the cluster. Spread over ~10 coordinators, each handles 30K/10 = 3K client ops/sec → 9K outbound RPCs/sec — comfortably within a single box's budget, and lets us scale the coordinator tier independently of storage. ## Trade-off A dedicated coordinator tier adds one network hop (2–6ms) and another thing to operate, in exchange for keeping clients thin and replicas focused on storage.

ring.name: Consistent-Hash Ring
ring.summary: Sorted map from 32-bit token → vnode → replica. Owns the placement function used by every read and write.

sections.heading: Data structure
sections.body: Sorted array of `(token, vnode_id, replica_id)` tuples. Lookup = binary search `upper_bound(hash(key))`, O(log V).

sections.heading: Preference list
sections.body: For replication factor N, walk clockwise from the token and collect the first N *distinct* physical replicas. Distinct-owner filter is what makes N physical-level copies (not N vnodes of one replica).

sections.heading: Why virtual nodes
sections.body: 150 vnodes per replica smooths load distribution — std-dev of ownership drops from ~50% (no vnodes) to ~5% (Dynamo paper fig 2).

sections.heading: Version pinning
sections.body: Each ring revision gets an integer version. Reads/writes include the coordinator's ring_version; replicas reject ops with a stale ring and the coordinator re-fetches — prevents split-brain during rebalance.

sections.heading: Multi-datacenter replication
sections.body: Book: 'Nodes in the same data center often fail at the same time due to power outages, network issues, natural disasters, etc. For better reliability, replicas are placed in distinct data centers, and data centers are connected through high-speed networks.' The preference-list walk takes **DC awareness** into account — at N=3, prefer one replica in each of 3 DCs so a DC outage loses at most one replica per key.

bottlenecks.title: Ring lookup hot-path CPU on coordinators under sustained QPS
bottlenecks.trigger: Every one of the 30K ops/sec does a ring.preference_list call before fan-out. With 6 replicas × 150 vnodes = 900 ring entries, binary search is O(log 900) ≈ 10 comparisons, plus a distinct-owner walk that may probe 5–10 vnodes to collect N=3 distinct replicas. At 3K ops/sec per coordinator this is ~45K–60K ring probes/sec/coord; if the ring is held behind a coarse RWLock that is write-locked during a gossip-driven ring_version bump, all in-flight lookups stall.
bottlenecks.symptom: Sharp latency spikes (10–50ms added to every PUT/GET) synchronized with ring-version changes; flame graphs show time in ring lock acquisition; p99 client latency correlates 1:1 with membership churn events even though no replica is actually down.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Make the ring immutable per version — publish a new fully-built sorted array on each version bump and swap an atomic pointer (copy-on-write); readers never lock. Cache the preference list per (token_bucket, ring_version) with a small LRU (e.g. 64K entries) to amortize the distinct-owner walk. Pre-materialize preference lists for all vnodes at ring-build time so lookup is a single binary search + array index.
bottlenecks.detection: Metric `ring.lookup_latency_ns` histogram per coordinator; alert when p99 > 100µs or when p99 rises >3× around a `ring.version_bump` event. Also track `ring.lock_wait_ns` — should be zero with COW.

bottlenecks.title: Distinct-owner walk degenerates under skewed vnode placement
bottlenecks.trigger: With only 6 physical replicas and 150 vnodes each (900 total), random token placement yields clusters where 4–6 adjacent vnodes belong to the same 1–2 replicas. The preference-list walk must skip these to collect N=3 *distinct* physical replicas, and with DC-awareness (prefer 1 replica per DC across 3 DCs) the walk can probe 15–30 vnodes in pathological hash neighborhoods before finding a valid N=3 set.
bottlenecks.symptom: Tail latency on ring lookup is 10–100× the median (e.g. median 2µs, p99.9 200µs); a small fraction of keys consistently take longer on every op; load distribution across replicas shows 15–20% std-dev instead of the expected ~5%.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Use a placement algorithm that enforces minimum spacing between same-owner vnodes (e.g. Cassandra's token allocator or rendezvous hashing with DC/rack constraints) rather than pure random token assignment; bump vnodes/replica from 150 → 256 to smooth distribution; precompute preference lists at ring-build time so the walk cost is paid once per ring version, not once per op.
bottlenecks.detection: Metric `ring.preference_walk_steps` histogram; alert if p99 > 10 steps. Also emit `ring.replica_ownership_fraction{replica=...}` at ring-build time and alert if any replica's ownership deviates >15% from 1/6.

bottlenecks.title: Ring-version adoption lag during gossip convergence causes STALE_RING storms
bottlenecks.trigger: Gossip converges in ~3s for 6 nodes (O(log N) × 1s rounds). During that window, some coordinators hold ring_version=N while replicas have already adopted N+1 (or vice versa) after a node join/leave or vnode rebalance. At 3K ops/sec per coord, a 2s divergence produces ~6K ops routed with the stale ring, each rejected with STALE_RING and retried — instantaneous 2× write amplification on the ring-lookup path and on coordinator fan-out.
bottlenecks.symptom: 100–500ms latency spikes and elevated error rate every time membership changes; logs show bursts of STALE_RING errors; retries consume coordinator concurrency budget (5000) and can cascade into HOL blocking on fan-out.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Piggyback ring diffs (not just version numbers) on gossip heartbeats so coordinators adopt the new ring before any op uses version N+1; allow replicas to serve under BOTH ring version N and N+1 for a 30s grace window instead of hard-rejecting; rate-limit rebalance vnode moves (e.g. 1 vnode/sec) to bound the blast radius of any single version bump.
bottlenecks.detection: Metric `ring.version_lag_seconds` = (cluster_max_version − local_version) per coordinator; alert when p99 > 5s. Track `coord.rpc.stale_ring_errors_total` rate; alert when >1% of ops over a 1-min window.

prebuild.explanation: ## Why the ring is here This KV store is **horizontally scaled** — 500 GB of logical data lives across 6 replicas, and every key needs to land on exactly 3 of them (N=3). Something has to answer the question "given key `cart:user42`, which 3 replicas own it?" — and it has to give the *same* answer on every coordinator, for every PUT and every GET, or writes and reads will miss each other. The ring is that answer. Consistent hashing specifically (vs. `hash(key) % 6`) is chosen because the cluster isn't static: gossip will eventually mark nodes DEAD, operators will add capacity, and when that happens you want to reshuffle ~1/6th of keys, not *all* of them. ## What happens without it If you used plain modulo hashing, adding a 7th replica remaps almost every key to a new owner. Clients read `cart:user42` and get an empty response because the value is physically on the old owner, which no longer "owns" that key. The user sees their cart wiped. The operator sees a healthy cluster quietly serving misses, and the anti-entropy worker starts frantically copying basically the entire dataset between replicas to catch up. ## The numbers At 30K ops/sec, the ring is consulted 30,000 times per second on the hot path. With 6 replicas × 150 vnodes = 900 tokens, lookup is a binary search: log₂(900) ≈ 10 comparisons, ~1µs — negligible next to the 3–10ms replica RPC. Cheap enough to do on every single op. ## Trade-off Vnodes smooth load (std-dev drops from ~50% to ~5%) but add a distinct-owner walk that can probe 5–10 entries in bad hash neighborhoods.

replica1.name: Replica 1 (Storage Node)
replica1.summary: LSM-backed storage node — writes hit WAL + memtable, reads hit memtable/SST, local Merkle tree kept in sync for anti-entropy.

sections.heading: Storage engine (Cassandra-style, book )
sections.body: RocksDB-style LSM (the book describes Cassandra's layout): commit log + memtable + on-disk SSTables + a Bloom filter per SSTable.

sections.heading: Write path
sections.body:
1. Append the write to the **commit log** on disk (durable).
2. Insert into the in-memory **memory cache (memtable)**.
3. Return ACK to the coordinator.
4. When memtable reaches a threshold, **flush to an SSTable** (sorted-string table of <key, value> pairs) on disk.

sections.heading: Read path
sections.body:
1. Check the memory cache (memtable) — if present, return.
2. On miss, consult the **Bloom filter** to decide which SSTables might contain the key.
3. Read candidate SSTables from disk; return the result.

sections.heading: Vector clock on every value
sections.body: Every stored value carries a vector clock `{replica_id: counter}`. Writes include the reader's context (the clock they observed). Conflicting clocks → store BOTH as siblings (don't overwrite).

sections.heading: Vector clock size bound
sections.body: Per book: the [server:version] list can grow unboundedly. Mitigation is a **threshold on the list length**; once exceeded, drop the oldest entries. The book notes Amazon has not encountered this in production, so it is considered an acceptable tradeoff.

sections.heading: Local Merkle tree
sections.body: Keyspace partitioned into leaves by hash prefix. Book suggests ~1M buckets per 1B keys (i.e. 1000 keys/bucket). Each leaf holds a rolling hash of (key, version) under it. Enables O(log N) comparison with peers during anti-entropy.

sections.heading: Hinted handoff buffer
sections.body: If a coordinator tags a write `for=replica3` because replica3 was down, this replica stores it under `hint:replica3:<key>` with a TTL and forwards on recovery.

gained: Lower read tail — no LSM compaction read amp
lost: Random write amplification hurts SSD endurance at high write QPS

bottlenecks.title: Compaction-driven write stalls and read amplification under sustained write load
bottlenecks.trigger: At 30K ops/sec × 20% writes = 6K writes/sec cluster-wide; with N=3 each replica absorbs ~6K writes/sec × 3/6 = 3K writes/sec of replicated PUTs plus read-repair and hinted-handoff replays. At ~1KB/value that's ~3 MB/s of memtable churn — a 128MB memtable flushes every ~40s, producing ~2K SSTables/day per replica. If leveled compaction falls behind (disk ~100 MB/s, compaction competing with live traffic), L0 SSTable count grows and every GET must probe more SSTables even with Bloom filters.
bottlenecks.symptom: Write latency p99 climbs from ~10ms to 100s of ms as memtable flushes back up waiting for L0 compaction; read latency tail grows because Bloom false-positive rate (~1%) × 20+ L0 SSTables means multiple disk seeks per GET; coordinator sees this replica as the straggler and fan-out HOL-blocks.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Use RocksDB leveled compaction with `level0_slowdown_writes_trigger=20` and `level0_stop_writes_trigger=36`; provision compaction threads = 4–8 and rate-limit foreground compaction I/O to ~60% of disk bandwidth (leaving headroom for live ops); size memtable to 256MB and keep ≥2 immutable memtables to absorb flush bursts; monitor and alert before stalls trigger.
bottlenecks.detection: Metrics `rocksdb.num-l0-files` (alert > 15), `rocksdb.stall-micros` rate (alert > 0 sustained), `rocksdb.pending-compaction-bytes` (alert > 10 GB); `replica.write_latency_ms` p99 per-replica with alert at 3× cluster median.

bottlenecks.title: Merkle tree maintenance cost on the hot write path
bottlenecks.trigger: Per book guidance of ~1000 keys/bucket, 500M keys / replica-share (~250M per replica at RF=3 across 6 nodes, so ~83M per replica) → ~83K Merkle leaves per replica. Every write must update the leaf hash for its bucket and propagate up log2(83K) ≈ 17 internal nodes. At 3K writes/sec/replica that's ~51K hash recomputations/sec just for Merkle maintenance, plus lock contention on hot buckets.
bottlenecks.symptom: Write path CPU dominated by Merkle updates during write bursts; anti-entropy runs see stale-looking trees if updates are deferred; if updates are synchronous, write p99 degrades; if async, a crash between WAL commit and Merkle update leaves the tree inconsistent with storage, causing spurious diffs and wasted repair bandwidth.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Update Merkle tree lazily — batch dirty-bucket marks on writes and recompute affected subtrees once per minute on a dedicated thread; persist a `dirty_bitmap` alongside WAL so recovery rebuilds only dirty buckets, not the whole tree; shard the tree across N locks so writes to different buckets don't contend.
bottlenecks.detection: Metric `replica.merkle.update_latency_ns` p99 on the write path (alert > 50µs); `replica.merkle.dirty_bucket_count` gauge (alert if stays > 10K for >5min, indicates recompute thread falling behind); correlation check between `antientropy.diff_bucket_count` and known write rate — unexplained diffs point to Merkle/storage skew.

bottlenecks.title: Unbounded vector-clock growth under churn and hinted handoff
bottlenecks.trigger: Book notes vclock entries can grow unboundedly — baseline is ~30B (3 entries), but during node churn, sloppy-quorum writes get tagged with hint-holder replica IDs, pushing vclocks to ~200B (10+ entries). A key written from many coordinators/replicas during a rolling restart can accumulate 10–20 entries per value; with 500M keys × 200B vclock = 100GB of vclock metadata vs the planned 500MB budget — a 200× overshoot.
bottlenecks.symptom: Unexpected storage growth (vclock metadata dwarfs value size for small values); reads return larger-than-expected payloads; sibling counts balloon because more-entry clocks are more likely to be pairwise-concurrent; SSTable size inflates, worsening compaction and Bloom memory footprint.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Implement book 's truncation: cap vclock to N_max=10 entries; when exceeded, drop the oldest (smallest-timestamp) entry and accept the rare false-concurrent it creates; prefer stable coordinator-replica identity over per-request IDs so entries don't fan out; run a background compaction task that prunes vclock entries for replicas absent from ring for >7 days.
bottlenecks.detection: Metric `replica.vclock.entries_per_value` histogram (alert p99 > 10); `replica.storage.vclock_bytes_total / replica.storage.value_bytes_total` ratio (alert > 0.2); track `replica.vclock.truncations_total` rate — a sudden rise signals churn-driven growth.

prebuild.explanation: ## Why a storage node like replica1 is here The whole point of this design is an **always-writable**, horizontally scaled KV store — which means the 500 GB of logical data has to physically live *somewhere*, and it has to live in more than one place so a single machine failure doesn't block writes. replica1 is one of those "somewheres." It's not special: it's one of 6 peer nodes, each holding a share of the keyspace plus copies of keys owned primarily by other nodes (that's what N=3 replication means). It runs the Cassandra-style write path from the book — commit log for durability, memtable for fast writes, SSTables for on-disk storage, Bloom filter to skip SSTables on reads — because that LSM shape is what lets a single box absorb thousands of writes per second without random-write disk thrash. ## What happens without it Remove replica1 and suddenly ~1/3 of all keys have only 2 surviving copies. With W=2, any *second* failure on those keys blocks writes entirely — the user sees "cart save failed," the operator sees quorum errors on the coordinator, and the anti-entropy worker starts frantically re-replicating to restore N=3. Lose two storage nodes in the same preference list and those keys are simply gone. ## The numbers At 30K ops/sec × 20% writes = 6K cluster writes/sec, each replicated 3×, spread over 6 nodes → each replica absorbs ~3K writes/sec ≈ 3 MB/s of memtable churn. A 128 MB memtable flushes every ~40s, producing manageable SSTable counts the compactor can keep up with. ## Trade-off Keeping the storage tier as symmetric peers (no primary) simplifies failover but means every node needs the full write path, Merkle tree, and hinted-handoff machinery.

replica2.name: Replica 2 (Storage Node)
replica2.summary: Identical in role to replica1; different position on the hash ring.

sections.heading: Symmetry
sections.body: No primary — for any given key, this node may be the first or third entry on the preference list depending on the hash. The ring decides per-key.

sections.heading: Replica role
sections.body: Accepts coordinator writes, participates in quorum reads, maintains its own Merkle tree for anti-entropy with peers.

bottlenecks.title: Hot-partition write skew when replica2 owns a trending key range
bottlenecks.trigger: Ring placement is per-key and asymmetric, so replica2 may sit at the head of the preference list for a vnode range containing a viral key (e.g. a flash-sale SKU cart or celebrity user). Cluster baseline is 6K writes/sec spread evenly (~3K writes/sec/replica at RF=3), but a hot range can concentrate 10–20× that on a single node, pushing replica2 past its serviceTimeMs=3–10ms envelope and its 2000-concurrency ceiling.
bottlenecks.symptom: replica2's write p99 jumps from ~10ms to 100–500ms while replica1/replica3 remain healthy; coordinators see replica2 as the straggler on fan-outs and W=2 quorums start relying on replica1+replica3, silently degrading durability for keys whose preference list is [replica2, X, Y]; hinted handoff buffers grow on neighbours even though replica2 is technically alive.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Enable per-key coordinator-side batching/coalescing (100ms debounce) for hot keys; add a request-admission gate on replica2 that sheds load above 80% of concurrency=2000; use key-level splitting (salt hot keys across sub-vnodes) or temporarily bump vnodes from 150→256 and re-shuffle the hot range; for genuinely hot single keys, switch the value type to a CRDT so writes are commutative and can be absorbed without sibling growth.
bottlenecks.detection: Per-replica `replica.write_qps{replica=replica2}` gauge with alert when it exceeds 2× cluster median; `replica.top_keys_by_write_rate` heavy-hitter sketch (alert on any key > 500 writes/sec); correlate `coord.rpc_latency_ms{replica=replica2}` p99 against replica1/replica3 — sustained 3× ratio signals skew, not node health.

bottlenecks.title: Asymmetric preference-list position amplifies recovery cost after replica2 restart
bottlenecks.trigger: Because ring positions are independent of replica identity, replica2 is the primary for ~1/6th of keys and the 2nd or 3rd copy for another ~1/3rd — roughly 250GB of its 500GB share. After a crash or rolling restart, all three roles must be caught up: commit-log replay (seconds), hinted-handoff drain from neighbours (at 2K hinted writes/sec × outage_minutes), and Merkle-diff repair against both peer replicas for every key range it participates in. A 10-minute outage produces ~1.2M hints plus Merkle diffs across ~28K leaves to compare against 2 peers.
bottlenecks.symptom: Post-restart, replica2 shows elevated write latency for 10–30 minutes as hint replay + anti-entropy repair + live traffic contend for disk (~100 MB/s ceiling); coordinators intermittently see R=2 reads return stale values on keys where replica2 is the 2nd responder but hasn't caught up; a second node failure during this window can drop some keys below W=2 quorum.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Throttle hint replay to ~10 MB/s per sender and anti-entropy repair to ~50 MB/s on the receiver; defer anti-entropy for 5 minutes after restart so commit-log replay + hint drain finish first; mark replica2 as NOT_READY in gossip until replay completes so coordinators prefer replica1/replica3 for reads during recovery; keep per-range catch-up watermarks so already-repaired ranges aren't re-scanned.
bottlenecks.detection: Metric `replica.recovery.hints_pending_bytes` and `replica.recovery.merkle_diff_bytes_remaining` on replica2; alert if either is non-zero >30 min post-restart. `replica.read_stale_responses_total` counter emitted when replica2 returns a vclock strictly dominated by peers during the recovery window.

bottlenecks.title: Commit-log fsync contention at 2000 concurrent writers
bottlenecks.trigger: replica2's sim declares concurrency=2000 and serviceTimeMs=3–10ms, implying up to 2000 in-flight PUTs each requiring a commit-log fsync before ACK. At 3K writes/sec steady-state plus burst traffic (hot-range events, hint replay), fsync queue depth on a single journal device saturates at ~200–500 group-commit batches/sec; further writers block waiting for fsync, not for memtable or network.
bottlenecks.symptom: Write latency p99 climbs with no corresponding CPU or memtable pressure; `iostat` shows journal device at 100% utilization with low bandwidth (small sync-heavy IOs); writes pile up in the coordinator's per-replica inflight queue, triggering the coordinator's HOL-blocking protection and causing W=2 fallbacks to replica1+replica3.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Enable group commit with a 1–2ms fsync batching window (amortize fsync across hundreds of writes); place commit log on a dedicated NVMe device separate from SSTables so compaction I/O doesn't contend; set commit-log segment size to 32MB and keep ≥2 segments pre-allocated; cap per-replica inflight at 500 at the coordinator to match realistic fsync throughput rather than the nominal 2000.
bottlenecks.detection: Metric `replica.commitlog.fsync_latency_ms` p99 (alert > 5ms) and `replica.commitlog.group_commit_batch_size` histogram (alert if p50 < 10, indicates batching not engaging); `replica.write_queue_depth` gauge (alert > 1000 sustained); journal device `iostat await` > 10ms.

prebuild.explanation: ## Why replica2 exists for *this* problem This is an **always-writable** KV store with N=3 replication and W=2/R=2 quorums. That math only works if there are actually three physical storage nodes holding every key — replica2 is the second of those three. It's not a backup or a standby; it's an equal peer that owns a live copy of ~1/3 of the keyspace as primary and participates in quorums for roughly another 2/3 as a secondary. The whole point of quorum-based consistency (W+R > N) collapses the moment you don't have N distinct machines to count acks from. ## What happens without it Delete replica2 and suddenly every key whose preference list included it has only 2 surviving copies. W=2 writes now require *both* remaining replicas to ack every single write — one GC pause on replica1 and writes start timing out. The user sees "cart save failed"; the operator sees quorum-failure errors spiking on the coordinator; the anti-entropy worker panics trying to re-replicate ~250 GB of data to restore N=3, saturating disk and pushing live traffic latency up with it. ## The numbers At 6K cluster writes/sec × RF=3 = 18K replica-writes/sec spread across 6 nodes → replica2 absorbs ~3K writes/sec ≈ 3 MB/s of memtable churn. Its 128 MB memtable flushes every ~40 s — well within a single disk's budget. Remove it and the other 5 nodes each have to absorb 18K/5 = 3.6K writes/sec *plus* the recovery re-replication traffic on top. ## Trade-off Symmetric peers (no primary) simplify failover but force every node to run the full write path, Merkle tree, and hinted-handoff machinery — no "cheap" replicas.

replica3.name: Replica 3 (Storage Node)
replica3.summary: Identical in role to replica1 and replica2; a third peer so we can tolerate one failure under N=3 / W=2 / R=2.

sections.heading: Why three replicas
sections.body: With N=3, W=2, R=2: W+R > N guarantees read-after-write on the latest quorum write, and we can lose any single replica without blocking writes OR reads. Two replicas would stop writes on any single failure.

sections.heading: Asymmetric placement
sections.body: Ring positions are independent of replica identity — this replica may hold the primary copy of some keys and the third copy of others. Load averages out via vnodes.

bottlenecks.title: Third-ack tail latency becomes write durability gap under W=2
bottlenecks.trigger: With W=2, coordinators ACK the client after replica1+replica2 and replica3's write completes asynchronously. At 6K cluster writes/sec × RF=3 / 6 nodes ≈ 3K writes/sec landing on replica3, any compaction stall, GC pause, or disk contention pushing replica3's p99 past the coordinator's 200ms async window causes the 3rd ack to be dropped or timed out. If replica3 is consistently the slow replica in a preference list, keys effectively live at RF=2 durability even though the cluster reports RF=3.
bottlenecks.symptom: On-call sees coordinator `async_ack_timeout` counters climbing for replica3 specifically; anti-entropy Merkle diffs against replica3 grow unexpectedly large (~MBs of divergent leaves per hour); a subsequent failure of replica1 or replica2 causes reads to return stale or missing values on a subset of keys whose 3rd ack to replica3 never completed.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Track every coordinator-initiated write with a durable hint if the 3rd ack misses a 500ms deadline — fall back to hinted handoff semantics even when the target is alive but slow; run anti-entropy against replica3 on a tighter 15-min cadence if its async-ack-success-rate drops below 99.9%; enforce a per-replica outbound queue cap (500 inflight) on coordinators so slow replica3 doesn't silently drop writes under backpressure.
bottlenecks.detection: Metric `coord.write.async_ack_latency_ms{replica=replica3}` p99 (alert > 100ms) and `coord.write.async_ack_missing_ratio{replica=replica3}` (alert > 0.1%); cross-check with `antientropy.diff_keys_total{peer=replica3}` — a sustained rise signals systematic 3rd-ack loss rather than random divergence.

bottlenecks.title: Correlated preference-list failure when replica3 shares a failure domain with replica1 or replica2
bottlenecks.trigger: The design mandates 1 replica per DC for N=3, but if rack/power/switch placement is not enforced within a DC, replica3 can share a ToR switch or power rail with one of its 2 preference-list peers for some vnodes. With per-replica failureRate=0.001 and 500M keys, ~1/3 of keys (~166M) have replica3 in their preference list; a correlated failure with replica1 or replica2 drops those keys below W=2/R=2 quorum simultaneously.
bottlenecks.symptom: A single ToR switch failure or power event takes out replica3 plus a peer, causing ~166M keys to become unwritable (W=2 blocks) and potentially unreadable (R=2 blocks) even though the cluster has 4 other healthy nodes; user sees cart-save failures concentrated on a keyspace slice; operator sees quorum-failure errors spike beyond the independent-failure math (10^-6) predicted by capacity estimates.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Enforce rack-aware placement in the ring builder — preference-list walk must collect N=3 replicas from distinct (DC, rack, power-domain) tuples, not just distinct replicas; validate placement invariant at every ring-version bump and refuse to publish a ring that violates it; deploy replica3 on a different rack/ToR from replica1 and replica2 at provisioning time and codify this in infra-as-code.
bottlenecks.detection: Ring-build invariant check: emit `ring.placement.shared_failure_domain_keys` — the count of keys whose preference list contains 2+ replicas in the same (rack, power) domain; alert if non-zero. Also track `cluster.correlated_replica_down_events_total` — any event where 2 replicas of a shared preference list go DEAD within 60s warrants a postmortem.

bottlenecks.title: Hinted-handoff replay storm overwhelms replica3 after transient outage
bottlenecks.trigger: If replica3 suffers a 30-min outage (e.g. rolling restart, kernel upgrade), neighbours buffer sloppy-quorum writes at ~2K hints/sec × 1800s ≈ 3.6M hints × ~1KB = ~3.6GB of hints across multiple senders. On recovery, all neighbours replay in parallel; combined inbound can exceed replica3's ~100 MB/s disk budget while it's also replaying its own commit log, running anti-entropy, and serving live traffic at 3K writes/sec.
bottlenecks.symptom: Post-restart, replica3 shows write p99 climbing to 100-500ms for 10-30 minutes; commit-log fsync queue saturates; coordinators mark replica3 as a straggler and fall back to W=2 with replica1+replica2, silently degrading durability; a second failure during this window drops affected keys below quorum.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Throttle per-sender hint replay to 10 MB/s with coordinator-side coordination (max 3 concurrent replaying senders into one target); mark replica3 as NOT_READY in gossip until commit-log replay finishes, then admit live traffic before opening the hint-replay floodgates; defer anti-entropy repair by 5 minutes post-restart so it doesn't compete with hint replay for the same disk bandwidth.
bottlenecks.detection: Metrics `replica.recovery.hints_inbound_bytes_per_sec` (alert > 50 MB/s sustained), `replica.commitlog.fsync_latency_ms` p99 (alert > 5ms during recovery window), and `replica.recovery.duration_seconds` (alert > 20 min — indicates replay storm, not normal recovery); dashboard correlating recovery metrics with live write latency for the same node.

prebuild.explanation: ## Why replica3 is here This design promises **always-writable** with quorum math: N=3 copies, W=2 writes must ack, R=2 reads must respond. That math only works if there are literally three physical machines holding every key. replica3 is the third one. It's not a hot spare or a backup — it's a full peer, doing live writes and reads exactly like replica1 and replica2. The *reason* there are three and not two is that W=2/R=2 with N=3 lets you lose any single replica and keep serving both reads and writes. Drop to N=2 and a single GC pause blocks every write to the affected keys. ## What happens without it Delete replica3 and every key whose preference list included it now has only 2 copies. W=2 writes require **both** survivors to ack every single PUT — one slow disk on replica1 and the user sees "cart save failed." The operator sees quorum-failure errors climbing on the coordinator while each individual node looks healthy. Meanwhile the anti-entropy worker starts frantically re-replicating ~250 GB of data to restore N=3, saturating disk bandwidth and pushing live write latency up alongside it. ## The numbers Cluster writes are 6K/sec × RF=3 = 18K replica-writes/sec spread across 6 nodes → each replica absorbs ~3K writes/sec ≈ 3 MB/s of memtable churn. Remove replica3 and the remaining 5 nodes each have to absorb 18K/5 = 3.6K writes/sec **plus** the recovery re-replication traffic layered on top — right when you can least afford it. ## Trade-off Three full peers triple your storage cost for a single-failure tolerance budget — the price of AP availability.

gossip.name: Gossip Membership
gossip.summary: Background protocol that propagates membership (alive/suspect/dead) and ring version across all nodes in O(log N) rounds.

sections.heading: Protocol
sections.body: Book describes the protocol: 'Each node maintains a node membership list … each node periodically increments its heartbeat counter … sends heartbeats to a set of random nodes, which in turn propagate to another set of nodes. If the heartbeat has not increased for more than predefined periods, the member is considered as offline.' In our sim: every 1s, each node picks k=3 random peers and exchanges `{ node_id, heartbeat_counter, state, ring_version, vnodes }`; SUSPECT at ~10s stale, DEAD at ~30s.

sections.heading: Two independent sources
sections.body: Book: 'it is insufficient to believe that a server is down because another server says so. Usually, it requires at least two independent sources of information to mark a server down.' Gossip provides this naturally — multiple peers confirm the stale heartbeat before DEAD is adopted.

sections.heading: Why gossip not all-to-all multicast
sections.body: Book notes all-to-all multicasting is inefficient at N nodes. Gossip converges in O(log N) rounds with per-node bandwidth O(k) — and has no central coordinator, so it survives network partitions with no SPOF.

sections.heading: Ring version propagation
sections.body: A new ring version (post-rebalance, post-join) piggybacks on heartbeats. Coordinators that see a new version re-fetch the authoritative ring once; replicas reject ops tagged with a stale version.

gained: Strong membership consistency — everyone sees the same view
Simpler to reason about during rebalances
lost: ZK itself is a dependency and a SPOF class
Cluster can't make membership progress during ZK outages

bottlenecks.title: False-positive DEAD marking under network jitter causes sloppy-quorum thrash
bottlenecks.trigger: With SUSPECT at ~10s stale and DEAD at ~30s, a transient network blip or GC pause on a replica that silently drops heartbeats for 30s flips it to DEAD across the cluster. At 6K writes/sec × 1/3 of keys owned by that replica = 2K writes/sec suddenly diverted to hinted-handoff neighbours; a 60s flap produces ~120K hints × ~1KB ≈ 120MB of hint buffer and a cascading repair burden on recovery.
bottlenecks.symptom: Coordinators abruptly stop routing to a healthy-but-slow replica; hinted-handoff buffers spike on its neighbours; on recovery, hint replay + anti-entropy storm elevates write p99 for 10+ minutes; on-call sees alternating DEAD/ALIVE gossip transitions (flapping) correlated with GC or network micro-outages rather than real failures.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Use a phi-accrual failure detector (per Cassandra) instead of fixed 10s/30s thresholds — it adapts to observed heartbeat variance; require 2 independent peer confirmations before DEAD adoption; add a 60s hysteresis before flipping back to ALIVE to damp flaps; rate-limit per-replica DEAD transitions to at most 1 per 5min.
bottlenecks.detection: Metric `gossip.state_transitions_total{node=...,to=DEAD}` rate — alert if any node flips more than 2× per hour; `gossip.heartbeat_age_seconds{node=...}` histogram and alert on p99 > 8s (pre-SUSPECT warning); correlate DEAD events with `coord.hints.pending_bytes` spikes to distinguish real failures from flaps.

bottlenecks.title: Convergence lag on larger clusters creates split-view windows during membership changes
bottlenecks.trigger: Gossip converges in O(log N) rounds × 1s per round — ~3s at 6 nodes, but scales to ~5–7s at 50+ nodes. With k=3 random peers per round and membership/ring-version piggybacked on heartbeats, a node join/leave creates a window where some coordinators see ring_version=N+1 while others still see N. At 30K ops/sec × 5s divergence = 150K ops routed with a stale ring across the cluster, each risking STALE_RING rejection + retry.
bottlenecks.symptom: Latency spikes (100–500ms) and elevated STALE_RING error rates synchronized with every node join/leave or rebalance; logs show bursts of ring-version mismatches; coordinator retry budget consumed, risking HOL blocking on fan-out concurrency=5000.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Increase gossip fan-out from k=3 to k=5 during active membership changes to accelerate convergence (roughly halves rounds-to-convergence); push a dedicated `ring_change` message out-of-band on the first round of a version bump rather than waiting for normal heartbeat piggyback; allow replicas to serve ops under both ring_version N and N+1 for a 30s grace window so divergence doesn't immediately produce rejects.
bottlenecks.detection: Metric `gossip.convergence_seconds` (time from first-node-adopts to last-node-adopts a new ring_version) — alert p99 > 10s; `gossip.ring_version_spread` gauge = max_version − min_version across cluster, alert if > 1 sustained over 10s; correlate with `coord.rpc.stale_ring_errors_total`.

bottlenecks.title: Heartbeat message bandwidth and CPU grow quadratically with cluster size
bottlenecks.trigger: Each gossip message carries the full membership list `{node_id, heartbeat_counter, state, ring_version, vnodes}`. With 150 vnodes/replica and ~100 bytes/entry including vnode tokens, a 6-node cluster message is ~600B (trivial), but a 50-node cluster message is ~5KB × k=3 peers × 1Hz per node = 50 × 15KB/s = 750KB/s cluster-wide gossip traffic, plus O(N²) CPU for merging membership vectors on every round. ServiceTimeMs=5–20 suggests merge is non-trivial even at 6 nodes.
bottlenecks.symptom: As the cluster grows, gossip CPU becomes a measurable tax on every node (1–5% per core); heartbeat processing latency climbs, delaying detection of real failures; bandwidth-constrained deployments (cross-DC links) see gossip compete with replication traffic.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Send compact gossip digests (node_id + heartbeat_counter only, ~16B/entry) and only exchange full state when digests disagree (SWIM-style piggyback); compress vnode tokens via delta encoding since they're stable; separate ring topology from heartbeat gossip — propagate ring_version over heartbeats but fetch the full ring lazily only when version changes; cap max message size and paginate membership across rounds at large scale.
bottlenecks.detection: Metric `gossip.message_bytes_sent_total` rate per node — alert if per-node gossip bandwidth exceeds 100KB/s; `gossip.merge_duration_ms` p99 (alert > 10ms); `gossip.cpu_seconds_total` — alert if gossip CPU exceeds 2% of a core sustained, signaling the protocol needs digest-based optimization.

prebuild.explanation: ## Why gossip is here for *this* problem This KV store is peer-to-peer by design — there's no master node, no ZooKeeper, nothing that says "here's the authoritative list of who's alive." But every coordinator needs that list on every single request: to build the preference list, to know which replica to skip when it's DEAD, to decide when to trigger sloppy-quorum hinted handoff. Gossip is how 6 peer nodes agree on membership *without* a central coordinator that would itself become a single point of failure. The AP stance ("always writable, even during partitions") would be meaningless if membership itself depended on a CP service that could go unreachable. ## What happens without it Imagine one replica crashes and nobody tells the coordinators. Every PUT still fans out to 3 replicas including the dead one, waits for its ack, and times out after ~200ms. The user sees every write take 200ms instead of 10ms; the operator sees coordinator concurrency budgets saturating even though 2 of 3 replicas are perfectly healthy; live traffic stalls behind dead-replica timeouts. Conversely, if coordinators disagreed about membership, some would route around the "dead" node while others kept sending — the cluster would behave inconsistently depending on which coordinator you hit. ## The numbers Book highlights why all-to-all heartbeating doesn't scale. At 6 nodes it's fine (30 links), but gossip converges in O(log N) rounds: log₂(6) ≈ 3 rounds × 1s = ~3s to propagate a membership change cluster-wide, with each node only talking to k=3 random peers per round instead of all 5. ## Trade-off Eventual membership consistency means there's always a brief window (~3s) where different coordinators see different views — the price of having no central authority.

antientropy.name: Anti-Entropy Worker
antientropy.summary: Periodic background job that compares Merkle trees between replica pairs and repairs divergent keys.

sections.heading: Why we need it
sections.body: Quorum writes, hinted handoff, and transient failures all leave rare divergences. Anti-entropy is the cleanup sweep — without it, stale replicas accumulate and read-repair alone can't catch cold keys.

sections.heading: Algorithm
sections.body:
Building the Merkle tree per book:
1. Divide the key space into buckets (bucket = root-level node, bounds tree depth).
2. For each bucket, hash each key with a uniform hash function.
3. Create a single hash node per bucket.
4. Build the tree upwards by hashing children, up to the root. Comparing two Merkle trees:
1. Compare root hashes; if equal → replicas are in sync, done.
2. If different, recurse into left/right children only where hashes differ.
3. Leaf-level differences point to the specific buckets that need syncing — transfer only those keys. Book: 'the amount of data needed to be synchronized is proportional to the differences between the two replicas, and not the amount of data they contain.'

sections.heading: Cost & throttling
sections.body: Runs once per hour per pair. Comparison is cheap (~MB of Merkle data); repair bandwidth is throttled to ~50 MB/s per replica so live traffic isn't affected.

sections.heading: Failure modes
sections.body:
- Mid-repair crash: the Merkle-diff is idempotent — resume from the top without harm.
- Flapping node: comparison against a node that's alternating up/down wastes CPU. Circuit-break pairs with high error rates.

lost: Cold keys stay divergent forever (never read → never repaired)
Slow-to-notice durability loss on long-tail keys

bottlenecks.title: Repair bandwidth saturates live traffic disk budget on divergent replicas
bottlenecks.trigger: After a multi-hour replica outage, recovery produces millions of divergent keys across thousands of Merkle leaves. At the configured 50 MB/s repair throttle per replica — half of the ~100 MB/s disk budget — anti-entropy competes directly with live writes (3K writes/sec/replica ≈ 3 MB/s memtable churn) and compaction I/O. A 1-hour outage yielding ~2K hints/sec × 3600s = 7.2M divergent keys × 1KB = ~7.2 GB of repair payload per pair, times 2 peers, takes ~5 min at the throttle — but coincides with hint-replay and commit-log replay contending for the same disk.
bottlenecks.symptom: Live write p99 climbs from ~10ms to 100-500ms on the receiving replica during repair windows; coordinators mark it as a straggler and HOL-block on fan-out; compaction falls behind, L0 SSTables accumulate, amplifying read latency as well; on-call sees a 'healthy' cluster with mysteriously elevated latency tied to anti-entropy schedule.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Adaptive throttling: cap repair bandwidth at 20 MB/s (not 50) when receiving replica's live write p99 exceeds 2× cluster median; defer anti-entropy by 5 min after any node restart so commit-log and hint replay finish first; stagger pair-wise repairs so no single replica is both a sender AND receiver in the same window; use `nice`/cgroup I/O priority to subordinate repair I/O to live traffic.
bottlenecks.detection: Metric `antientropy.repair_bytes_per_sec{replica=...}` and correlation with `replica.write_latency_ms` p99 — alert if repair-active windows show p99 > 3× repair-idle baseline. Track `antientropy.repair_duration_seconds` histogram; alert if p99 > 30min (indicates repair backlog). `rocksdb.num-l0-files` rising during repair signals compaction starvation.

bottlenecks.title: Merkle tree comparison amplifies under high-churn keyspaces producing spurious diffs
bottlenecks.trigger: Merkle leaves hash (key, version) tuples, so every vclock update — even for a value that eventually converges — dirties the leaf. With ~83K leaves per replica (1000 keys/bucket per book ) and 3K writes/sec/replica, ~3% of leaves dirty per second; across an hour between anti-entropy runs, essentially every leaf has changed at least once. Two replicas running slightly different write orders will show divergent leaf hashes even when their actual (key, value) sets are identical post-reconciliation, forcing key-level comparison on all ~83K leaves.
bottlenecks.symptom: Anti-entropy pair comparison reports thousands of 'divergent' leaves per run but repair transfers find most keys already in sync; wasted CPU and network (~MB of key-list exchange per leaf); repair worker `concurrency=50` saturates on false-positive leaves while real divergences wait in queue; `antientropy.diff_leaves_total` appears alarmingly high but data is actually consistent.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Hash leaves over (key, vclock-descriptor) where descriptor is order-independent (e.g. sorted vclock entries, not insertion order); run read-repair inline on GETs to reconcile hot keys before anti-entropy sees them; increase anti-entropy cadence from 1h to 15min on high-churn ranges so per-run diff volume stays bounded; short-circuit leaf comparison when both sides' key-counts match and a sampled key agrees.
bottlenecks.detection: Metric `antientropy.diff_leaves_total` vs `antientropy.keys_actually_repaired_total` per run — alert if ratio > 10:1 (mostly spurious). Track `antientropy.leaf_comparison_duration_ms` p99; alert > 200ms (matches the sim's serviceTimeMs ceiling, indicating pathological cases).

bottlenecks.title: Worker concurrency ceiling stalls repair under correlated multi-pair divergence
bottlenecks.trigger: With 6 replicas there are C(6,2)=15 possible pairs, but each replica has only 2 peers to repair with (its N-1 preference-list neighbors for the ranges it shares). Worker `concurrency=50` and `serviceTimeMs=20-200ms` per leaf comparison means ~250-2500 leaves/sec throughput per worker. After a cluster-wide event (network partition heal, DC reconnection) where all 6 replicas have drifted from all their peers simultaneously, 12 active pair-repairs compete for the 50-slot concurrency budget plus the 0.2% per-op failure rate causes retries that further consume slots.
bottlenecks.symptom: Anti-entropy backlog grows — `pending_repair_pairs` queue depth climbs; some replica pairs go hours or days without a successful comparison after a major event; cold keys stay divergent indefinitely because read-repair never touches them and anti-entropy can't catch up; durability guarantee silently degrades on a long-tail keyspace slice.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Raise worker concurrency to 200 and scale horizontally (run anti-entropy as multiple worker instances coordinated via leader election on repair pairs); prioritize pairs by last-successful-repair age so the oldest divergences are addressed first; circuit-break repeatedly failing pairs (exponential backoff) so 0.2% failure rate doesn't compound into retry storms; after cluster-wide events, temporarily boost concurrency to 500 for a 1-hour catch-up window.
bottlenecks.detection: Metric `antientropy.pair_last_successful_repair_age_seconds` per pair — alert if any pair exceeds 4h (4× nominal 1h cadence). Track `antientropy.worker_concurrency_utilization` — alert > 80% sustained, signals backlog building. `antientropy.pairs_pending_gauge` with alert > 20 (above steady-state 15).

prebuild.explanation: ## Why anti-entropy is here for *this* problem This KV store is AP: it keeps accepting writes during failures using **sloppy quorum** and **hinted handoff**. Those mechanisms are great at *availability* but they accumulate small divergences — a replica was briefly down, a hint expired before delivery, a W=2 write never reached the 3rd replica, a network blip dropped a replicated PUT. Read-repair fixes these as keys are read, but cold keys (the long tail nobody GETs for weeks) never get touched. Without a sweep, those divergences silently pile up until you've quietly lost a copy of some keys and don't know it — which defeats the whole point of N=3. ## What happens without it Imagine replica3 missed a few thousand writes during a 10-minute network partition. Hinted handoff replayed most, but ~50 expired. Months later replica1 dies for real. Reads that used to quorum on {r1, r2} now quorum on {r2, r3} — and for those 50 cold keys, r3 still has stale data. The user sees their year-old shopping cart revert. The operator sees no error at all — quorum was satisfied, just with stale data. Durability has been silently compromised. ## The numbers Capacity budgets ~83K Merkle leaves per replica (500M keys / 1000 per bucket / ~6 nodes). Comparing two trees: start at the root, recurse only where hashes differ. A pair with 100 divergent keys touches ~log₂(83K) ≈ 17 levels × a handful of nodes per level ≈ ~100 hash comparisons — not 83K. The book's point: *comparison cost scales with divergence, not dataset size*. That's what makes hourly sweeps feasible at 500GB. ## Trade-off You pay steady background CPU + ~50 MB/s repair bandwidth in exchange for catching the rare divergences read-repair can't.

operations.title: PUT with W=2 quorum (happy path)
operations.name: PUT with W=2 quorum (happy path)
operations.description: Client writes `cart:user42 → [item A]` with a vector-clock context. Coordinator fans out to all 3 replicas; once W=2 acks arrive it replies to the client. The 3rd ack finishes asynchronously.

steps.title: Client issues PUT with context
steps.action: Client includes the vector clock it last observed for this key. On first write for a new key, the context is empty.

steps.title: Coordinator hashes key and consults the ring
steps.action: MurmurHash3 of the key yields a 32-bit token. Coordinator asks the ring for the N=3 preference list.
steps.codeOrCommand:
token = murmur3_32("cart:user42") # 0x91C3_22BE
pref = ring.preference_list(token, N=3)
# → [replica1, replica2, replica3]

steps.title: Ring returns preference list
steps.action: Binary search + distinct-owner walk. Preference list is stable as long as ring version is unchanged.
steps.codeOrCommand:
idx = upper_bound(ring.tokens, 0x91C322BE)
owners = for i in range(len(ring)): r = ring.replica_at((idx + i) % len(ring)) if r not in owners: owners.append(r) if len(owners) == 3: break
return owners
steps.note: Exactly N distinct replicas are returned — distinct-owner filter prevents replicas landing on adjacent vnodes of one node.

steps.title: replica1 bumps its counter and runs the book's write path
steps.action: The primary for this key follows the book Cassandra-style write path: (1) append to commit log on disk, (2) insert into memory cache (memtable), (3) ACK. SSTable flush happens later when the memtable crosses a threshold.
steps.codeOrCommand:
# book write path
vc = incoming.context.copy
vc["replica1"] = vc.get("replica1", 0) + 1 # → 4 # 1. persist on commit log
commit_log.append(Put("cart:user42", value, vc))
commit_log.fsync # 2. insert into memtable (memory cache)
memtable.put("cart:user42", (value, vc)) # 3. ACK; memtable will be flushed to an SSTable later
return ACK

steps.title: replica2 commits replica write (parallel)
steps.action: Same local write path as replica1. This is the 2nd ack — satisfies W=2.
steps.codeOrCommand:
wal.append(Put("cart:user42", value, vclock))
wal.sync
memtable.put("cart:user42", (value, vclock))
return ACK

steps.title: replica3 commits asynchronously (late ack)
steps.action: Ack arrives after the coordinator has already replied to the client. Still written durably.
steps.codeOrCommand:
wal.append(Put("cart:user42", value, vclock))
wal.sync
return ACK

steps.title: Coordinator collects W=2 acks and returns
steps.action: As soon as 2 of 3 replicas ack, coordinator returns success with the new vector clock. The 3rd ack completes in the background.
steps.decision: W quorum satisfied with replica1+replica2; replica3 finishes asynchronously.

steps.title: Client receives OK with new vclock
steps.action: Client stores the returned vclock as the context for this key's next write. Typical latency 8–20ms.

operations.title: GET with R=2 quorum (consistent read)
operations.name: GET with R=2 quorum (consistent read)
operations.description: Client reads `cart:user42`. Coordinator fans out to all 3 replicas, waits for R=2 to respond, compares vector clocks: if one dominates the other, return it; if equal, return it; if concurrent, return siblings.

steps.title: Client issues GET
steps.action: Client requests the latest value for the key.

steps.title: Coordinator hashes and consults ring
steps.action: Same hash + ring lookup as the write — reads and writes see the same preference list for a given key under a stable ring.
steps.codeOrCommand:
token = murmur3_32("cart:user42")
pref = ring.preference_list(token, N=3) # [replica1, replica2, replica3]

steps.title: Ring returns preference list
steps.action: Returns the same 3 replicas the write landed on.

steps.title: replica1 runs the book's read path (memtable → bloom → SSTables)
steps.action: Book read path: check the memory cache (memtable) first; if absent, consult the Bloom filter to pick candidate SSTables, then read from disk. Returns value + its stored vector clock.
steps.codeOrCommand:
# book read path
hit = memtable.get("cart:user42")
if hit is not None: return hit # Bloom filter → which SSTables might contain the key?
candidates = [sst for sst in sstables if sst.bloom.might_contain("cart:user42")]
for sst in candidates: found = sst.lookup("cart:user42") if found is not None: return found
return None

steps.title: replica2 reads in parallel
steps.action: Same local read path. Second response satisfies R=2.

steps.title: Coordinator compares vclocks, R=2 satisfied
steps.action: Both responses carry the same vclock → no conflict. Return the value without waiting for replica3.
steps.codeOrCommand: def reconcile(responses): clocks = [r.vclock for r in responses] if all(c == clocks[0] for c in clocks): return responses[0].value # equal dominant = find_dominant(clocks) if dominant is not None: return responses[dominant].value # one clock covers all others return siblings(responses) # concurrent — return all

stateAfter.decision: R=2 satisfied, vclocks equal, return value

steps.decision: R=2 met with equal vclocks — no conflict resolution needed.

steps.title: Client receives value and vclock
steps.action: Typical latency 5–12ms. Client stores the returned vclock for any subsequent write on this key.

operations.title: Concurrent writes detected → return siblings
operations.name: Concurrent writes detected → return siblings
operations.description: Two clients write the same key in parallel, each with a vclock neither of which dominates the other. The coordinator on read returns BOTH values as siblings so the client can merge them application-side.

steps.title: Client A writes cart:user42 = [A]
steps.action: Client A issues a PUT with context vclock `{replica1: 3}`. Coordinator lands the write on replica1 (W=1 for this illustration).

steps.title: replica1 stores value with vclock {replica1: 4}
steps.action: replica1 increments its counter to 4 and stores Client A's write. Other replicas have not yet received it (network delay).

steps.title: replica2 simultaneously receives Client B's write
steps.action: A DIFFERENT client (B) read the key earlier with context `{replica1: 3}` and now writes a different value — landing on replica2 before replica2 saw Client A's write. replica2 bumps its own counter.
steps.note: Client B's context was `{replica1: 3}` — replica2 records this history PLUS its own increment.

steps.title: Later, Client C issues GET
steps.action: A third client reads the key. The coordinator fans out to all three replicas.

steps.title: Coordinator fans out read to all 3 replicas
steps.action: Classic read-time reconciliation — coordinator collects all 3 responses before returning since vclocks disagree.
steps.codeOrCommand:
responses = await_all([replica1, replica2, replica3])
# r1: (value=[A], vc={replica1: 4})
# r2: (value=[B], vc={replica1: 3, replica2: 1})
# r3: (value=, vc={replica1: 3}) # cold replica, lagged

steps.title: replica1 returns [A] with vclock {replica1: 4}
steps.action: Its write has the A value.

steps.title: replica2 returns [B] with vclock {replica1: 3, replica2: 1}
steps.action: Its write has the B value. The vclock is NEITHER dominated by nor dominates replica1's.

steps.title: replica3 returns stale value (will be dropped in reconciliation)
steps.action: replica3 hadn't received either write yet. Its vclock `{replica1: 3}` is strictly dominated by both siblings → safely dropped.

steps.title: Coordinator detects concurrent vclocks → return siblings
steps.action: Coordinator compares the 3 clocks. replica3's is dominated → drop. replica1's and replica2's are CONCURRENT (neither dominates the other) → return both as siblings and let the client merge.
steps.codeOrCommand:
# Prune dominated clocks
live = for r in responses: if not any(strictly_dominates(other.vc, r.vc) for other in responses): live.append(r)
# live = [r1, r2] if len(live) == 1: return live[0].value
else: return Siblings([r.value for r in live], merged_vc=merge(live))

stateAfter.decision: 2 concurrent siblings — return both with merged vclock for next write context

steps.decision: Concurrent writes detected — return siblings instead of silently overwriting.

steps.title: Client receives siblings and merges application-side
steps.action: Client C gets BOTH `[A]` and `[B]`. It runs the user-supplied merge function (for a shopping cart, union → `[A, B]`) and writes the result back with the merged vclock. That single reconciled write propagates through the cluster and ends the conflict.
steps.note: Siblings are the Dynamo-style AP tradeoff made visible: the store refuses to silently pick a winner because only the application knows the correct merge semantics. A counter would take max, a set would union, etc.

tradeoffs.rationale: Shopping carts and session stores must stay writable during partitions; callers who need strong reads opt into W + R > N per operation.
LWW silently loses concurrent updates; vector clocks surface siblings so the application merges correctly, with LWW as the cap when siblings explode.

tradeoffs.chosen: Synchronous to W, asynchronous to N
tradeoffs.rationale: W acks give the durability guarantee the client needs; the remaining replicas catch up in the background via read-repair and anti-entropy.

tradeoffs.decision: Commit log + memtable + SSTable (LSM) vs B-tree (update-in-place)
tradeoffs.rationale: LSMs turn random writes into sequential log appends — the right fit for write-heavy KV workloads; B-trees win only for update-heavy OLTP.
Gossip removes the strongly-consistent dependency that would become a single point of failure; convergence in O(log N) seconds is fast enough.

tradeoffs.decision: Strict quorum vs sloppy quorum + hinted handoff
tradeoffs.rationale: During single-node outages, accepting the write on a neighbour with a hint preserves availability without violating durability once the hint is replayed.
